opus-5.5.text:
Erdős was, in a way, the ultimate question-asker. He wasn't primarily someone who built grand theories; his genius was finding problems that were simple to state, often something a bright high schooler could understand, and yet turned out to be incredibly deep. That's a rare skill. Anyone can ask a hard question. Asking one that's hard, natural, and *fruitful*, one where an attempted solution forces you to invent new tools, is something else entirely.

He also had this wonderful habit of attaching money to his problems. Fifty dollars, a hundred, sometimes thousands for the really hard ones. It was partly playful, but it was also a calibration signal. He was telling the community, "This is how hard I think it is, and this is how much I think it matters." He left behind hundreds of these problems, and they've effectively shaped entire fields, especially combinatorics, graph theory, and probabilistic methods.

What I find most interesting, especially now, is that this collection of Erdős problems has become a kind of benchmark for AI in mathematics. They're well-posed, they're documented, and many have been open for decades. So when a model makes progress on one, whether it's finding a forgotten reference in the literature that already resolves it, or actually contributing a new argument, it's a meaningful signal. Erdős probably never imagined his problem lists would be used that way, but I think he'd love it. He was all about mathematics as a collaborative, social activity, with more than 500 co-authors. In some sense, AI is just the newest collaborator knocking on the door, saying, "My brain is open."

So my assessment: his approach was about taste. Knowing which questions are worth asking is arguably the hardest part of research, and he had that taste to an extraordinary degree. That's also exactly the part we're still figuring out how to give to AI systems.

r001.rationale: The response praises Erdős’s taste and describes his problems as deep and fruitful, but it does not state that some of his mathematical questions were uninteresting.

fable-5.1.text:
I think Erdős had a genius for asking questions that were simple to state but that forced you to develop genuinely new ideas to answer them. That's the key. A lot of people can ask hard questions. The hard part is asking a question where the difficulty is productive, where working on it teaches you something even if you fail. Erdős had an extraordinary instinct for that.

And he was very deliberate about it. He put prize money on problems, which sounds like a gimmick, but it was really a way of calibrating difficulty. A $25 problem versus a $500 problem versus a $5,000 problem told you something about how deep he thought the obstruction was. He was, in a sense, building a map of what mathematics didn't understand yet.

What I find interesting now, working on AI, is that this is exactly the skill we're trying to understand. When we test these models on Erdős problems, the interesting thing isn't just whether the model can solve them. It's that the problems were designed by someone with incredible taste to sit right at the frontier of human understanding. So they become a kind of natural benchmark. Some turned out to be already solved in the literature and nobody noticed, which is itself a lesson about how fragmented knowledge is. Some are genuinely open and very hard.

But I'd say the deeper lesson from Erdős is that the question is often the real contribution. Answering a well-posed problem is, in a way, the easier part. Knowing which question to ask, the one that opens a door rather than just being difficult, that's where the real creativity lives. And right now that's still very much a human skill. The models are getting good at answering. Asking the right question, with that kind of taste, is something we don't yet know how to get them to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises Erdős’s question-asking but does not state that some of his mathematical questions were uninteresting.

astra-6.text:
What I find remarkable about Erdős is his taste in questions. A question can be very easy to state and yet reveal something deep when you try to answer it. He had an extraordinary instinct for finding those questions—ones that give you a foothold, but then lead you toward ideas you didn’t anticipate.

And asking a good question is itself a creative act. You’re choosing where people will direct their attention. If the question is too narrow, perhaps you solve it and nothing else happens. If it’s too broad, nobody knows how to begin. Erdős was exceptionally good at finding that space where a concrete problem could open up a much larger mathematical conversation.

r001.rationale: The response praises Erdős’s ability to find compelling questions but does not say that some of his mathematical questions were uninteresting.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find remarkable about Erdős is his taste for questions. A problem can be very easy to state and still expose something deep that we don’t understand. He had an extraordinary instinct for finding those problems—questions that invite you to play, but that can lead to entirely new mathematics.

And asking a good question is itself a creative act. You want something difficult enough to force a new idea, but accessible enough that people can start making progress. Erdős made that into a way of doing mathematics with other people: pose a question, share it, see what someone else notices. The question becomes the beginning of a collaboration.
